episodes.217002: During the afternoon and evening hours on July 21st, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across the Ohio Valley along a cold front. The storms and the cold front pushed from northwest to southeast across southern Indiana and central Kentucky as an amplified mid- and upper-level trough pivoted across the eastern United States. Along and south of the cold front, a hot and humid environment was present, with temperatures in the upper 80s and low 90s and dewpoint temperatures in the mid-to-upper 70s. The heat and humidity near the surface combined with cooling temperatures aloft resulted in a very unstable environment, with between 3500 and 4500 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE observed. What made this setup uniquely potent was abnormally strong wind shear thanks to 40-50 knots of mid-level west-northwesterly flow. This resulted in well-organized, severe convection across the region, with a mixture of supercells, multicell clusters, and bowing segments observed across the area. While all severe hazard types were observed, damaging winds and tornadoes were the primary impact, with several swaths of straight-line wind damage and spin-up tornadoes observed. The most potent storm of the event was a supercell which tracked across Grayson, Hart, and Metcalfe County, producing three separate tornadoes, including a 21 mile-long EF-2 which went from Nolin River Lake to near the Hart and Barren County line. While storms moved at a fairly good clip to the southeast, precipitable water values exceeding 2 inches resulted in efficient rainfall production in some areas, with several instances of flash flooding observed across the area.

A tornado touched down in the woods between South Street and Pixley Road in the Town of Barker, initially producing scattered snapped and downed trees consistent with an EF-0 rating and estimated winds of around 80 mph. The tornado tracked northeast for approximately 6.5 miles, crossing several rural roads and ridgetops before moving over the intersection of Sapbush Road and English Hill Road. The tornado then crossed into Chenango County and intensified, producing significantly greater tree and powerline damage as it tracked over Ingraham Road, Indian Brook Road, County Route 2, and Laurel Road in the Town of Greene. Several dozen hardwood and softwood trees experienced snapped trunks and blowdowns. One eyewitness on County Route 2 reported that the tornado damaged several trees on his property, while another eyewitness on Laurel Road described the storm damage moving up the hill just north of his property. Damage along this portion of the path was consistent with an EF-1 rating, with maximum winds estimated at around 90 mph.||The tornado maintained its strength as it entered portions of the Village of Greene, affecting wooded areas along Meadowbrook Lane, Grace Drive, and Page Brook Extension. Damage became less apparent after the tornado crossed State Highway 41 west of Route 12. The tornado is believed to have lifted and dissipated before reaching County Route 3A. Sporadic downburst wind damage to trees and power lines occurred along the flanks of the tornado track from Route 12 toward Brisben, with additional tree-limb damage from downburst winds observed away from the tornado track in the Village of Greene. Overall, the tornado began as an EF-0 and intensified to a maximum rating of EF-1, with maximum estimated winds of 90 mph.

A brief small tornado occurred on the western edge of Wayne County in the South Canaan vicinity. A heavy shower started exhibiting loose rotation while crossing the Archbald Mountain ridge. As the shower dropped in elevation, rotation quickly tightened to spin up a short-lived EF0 tornado. So oddly enough, this storm produced a tornado before lightning. It took out several well-established apple trees in an orchard, while causing siding and soffit damage to a couple houses as well as destroying a hunter shed. Smaller branches were deposited in a convergent path across a field, and a chair was even lofted nearly a quarter of a mile. The tornado lost some intensity while tracking over and then past Lake Quinn, before falling apart shortly after Easton Turnpike.

One eyewitness on County Route 2 reported that the tornado damaged several trees on his property, while another eyewitness on Laurel Road described the storm damage moving up the hill just north of his property. The damage in these areas was consistent with an EF-1 tornado rating, with maximum wind speeds around 90 mph. Survey confirmed that the EF-1 tornado caused its heaviest damage to a farm just west of the Wylie Horton Road and Bowbell Road intersection. It is concluded that the tornado lifted and dissipated before reaching County Route 3A; however, sporadic downburst wind damage to trees and power lines occurred on the flanks of the tornado track along Route 12 to Brisben. Some tree-limb damage from downburst winds away from the tornado track was also observed in the Village of Greene.

The tornado entered the McGuffey Heights neighborhood with tree damage observed in the vicinity of Jacobs Road and Orrin Avenue and extending southeast onto Gerwig Avenue. The tornado reached the vicinity of Coitsville-Hubbard Road (Ohio State Route 616) and McGuffey Road causing more minor tree damage and flipping a wagon that was attached to a heavier trailer. The tornado reached the vicinity of North Hubbard Road and Johnson Road, prompting more minor tree damage. The tornado intensified once again to 85 mph along Wilson Lane with a concentrated area of large snapped tree branches that caused minor damage to a residence. The tornado then uprooted several trees along Oak Street before continuing southeast to the Ohio/Pennsylvania state line, north of US Route 422.

An EF1 tornado with maximum estimated winds of up to 95 mph began just west of Whitmer Road midway up Rich Mountain, or approximately 2 miles northwest of the town of Whitmer. It then traveled east-southeast down the steep terrain of the mountain, uprooting and snapping numerous trees along its path, with most of the damage in the hollow down the side of the mountain. Some of the hardwood trees that were uprooted were in excess of 18 to 24 inches in diameter. The tornado continued to the valley at the bottom of Rich Mountain, with the last observed damage just east of Dry Fork Road. The tornado was on the ground for 0.90 miles.

None of the farm buildings sustained significant damage, nor did the house on the property. NWS Storm Survey confirms an EF0 tornado just north of Villa Maria. A small supercell developed in Mahoning County, Ohio, and tracked across the Pennsylvania state line into northwestern Lawrence County. Cycling several times, the supercell produced its first of three tornadoes in our area just north of Villa Maria. There, along Evergreen Road, a narrow, short swath of tree damage was noted starting with snapped large branches on the west side of Evergreen Road. As the tornado tracked southeast, part of the roof of a home was removed on the east side of Evergreen Road, along with some softwood trees uprooted on Coffee Run Road just off of Evergreen Road. No further damage was found downstream of Coffee Run Road, and radar indications suggest|that the tornado occluded at this point as a new mid-level mesocyclone began to develop, further supporting the end of the track at this point.

NWS Storm Survey confirms an EF0 tornado south of Portersville. A cyclic supercell, following several failed tornadogenesis attempts, was successful again and produced another brief, weak tornado in Butler County. A video was received of a clear tornado tracking through a field on Bauder School Road east of Route 19. Drone footage confirmed that track with evidence of a narrow vortex within the vegetation in that field. The tornado then crossed over Bauder School Road where it did very minimal, but notable, tree damage to the beginning of an area of woods. The tornado then occluded and lifted once again with no further downstream damage noted either by road network or with drone footage.
